scenes.vo: I'm Rifat, from Cambridge in the United Kingdom. This is Part 1 of three. Part 1 is the real process. Part 2 shows the AI automation I built to run it, and Part 3 shows how it ends.
scenes.ph: Face cam placeholder · lower-third: Rifat · Cambridge, UK

scenes.label: CHAPTER 1
scenes.title: The goal
scenes.broll: Goal infographic, the three-step process highlighted
scenes.vo: Here's the goal. Company debt stays the company's. Liquidation hands the company to a licensed practitioner, who sells the assets and pays creditors in order. Generally, the director isn't personally liable.
overlay: 1 Hand over  →  2 Sell assets  →  3 Pay creditors in order

scenes.label: CHAPTER 2
scenes.title: Five things to do first
scenes.broll: On-screen numbered list 1 to 5, HMRC screen for step 1 (S2)
scenes.vo: Five things to do first. One: check your HMRC balance. Mine is £39,475.54. Two: gather the company's books and records. Mine are in a storage unit, and I'm only paying for it until I get access to the documents. Three: get a licensed insolvency practitioner. I chose one with 4.8 stars on Trustpilot. Four: stop trading, and don't pay one creditor ahead of the others. Your practitioner will confirm this. Five: close your invoices and bring every bank account to zero, or the money goes to the Crown. I've recovered both outstanding customer invoices, £2,203.17 in total, and that's everything I received from my customers.
overlay: 5 Close invoices, banks to zero (£2,203.17 recovered)

scenes.label: CHAPTER 3
scenes.title: What it costs and how long it takes
scenes.broll: Cost and timeline graphic: £1,500 + £2,100, five stages, Gazette wait
scenes.vo: Here's what it costs, and how long it takes. A £1,500 deposit, then a £2,100 balance. I've paid both. There are five stages: the deposit, the information pack, the board meeting, the liquidator taking over, and finally the banks at zero and the Gazette notice, followed by a wait of about two months. In my case, I signed Stage 3 on 30 October, the creditors are notified on 19 November, and the proposed liquidation date is 2 December.
overlay: Stage 3 signed 30 Oct · creditors 19 Nov · liquidation 2 Dec

scenes.label: CHAPTER 4
scenes.title: The exceptions
scenes.broll: Four exception cards on screen, red accent
scenes.vo: Now the exceptions, because this matters. The protection isn't absolute. A director can still be personally liable for wrongful or fraudulent trading, for personal guarantees, for an overdrawn director's loan account, and for paying one creditor ahead of the others. That's why the practitioner decides, not me.

scenes.label: CHAPTER 5
scenes.title: What my emails taught me
scenes.broll: Email timeline graphic (S12): chase reminders, the receipt, the liquidation-date email (names and addresses blurred)
scenes.vo: Three lessons from my own emails. One: the process stops until the balance is paid. My provider chased me six times, so don't leave it to the end. Two: answer everything in writing, and keep a list of what's still outstanding. I still owe my provider a few records before 19 November. Three: your records are part of the process. Mine are in a storage unit and on Drive, and the practitioner arranges the collection.
overlay: 2 Answer in writing, list what is outstanding
3 Records are part of the process

scenes.label: CHAPTER 6
scenes.title: How I keep track of it
scenes.broll: n8n canvas, 20 seconds (S3), then the dashboard (S10)
scenes.vo: I keep track of all of it with an n8n workflow and a few AI agents: a planner, a risk checker and a director. I type what I'm trying to do, and I get a plan and a risk list back. Part 2 shows exactly how it's built, and the workflow is free to import.
